blocks.html: After studying this chapter you will be able to:

items.html: define software and distinguish a program from software
classify software into system, application and programming software
describe operating systems, device drivers, utilities, firmware and language translators
name types of application software with examples
explain proprietary, freeware, shareware, open-source, OEM and subscription licences
install, update and uninstall software correctly
describe the stages of software development

blocks.html: A new computer without software is like a new phone without a SIM card or apps — the hardware is there but it can do nothing useful.
Definition: Software is a set of programs, data and documentation that tells the hardware what to do. A program is a single set of instructions written to do a particular task.
For example, MS Office is software; Excel, Word and PowerPoint are programs within it, along with help files, templates and settings.

rows: Helps the user do a specific job
Runs on its own after booting
Low-level and system languages such as C, C++ and assembly

blocks.html: A third category, programming software (development tools), helps programmers create software: code editors, compilers, debuggers and IDEs such as Code::Blocks and Visual Studio.
The operating system (OS) manages the processor, memory, files, devices and security, and provides the user interface (see the Class 9 book for details). It has two main parts:

items.html: Kernel — the core that talks directly to the hardware.
Shell — the interface through which users give commands (a GUI desktop or a command line).

blocks.html: A short history of Linux: In 1987 Professor Andrew Tanenbaum wrote MINIX, a small Unix- like OS for teaching. Inspired by it, a Finnish student, Linus Torvalds, started writing his own kernel in 1991 and shared it freely on the internet. Thousands of volunteers improved it, and today Linux runs most of the world's servers and supercomputers, and its kernel is the base of Android.

A device driver is a small program that lets the OS communicate with a particular hardware device — printer, scanner, graphics card, Wi-Fi card. Plug and Play (PnP) means the OS detects a new device and installs its driver automatically when you plug it in.

rows: Deletes temporary and unnecessary files to free space
Rearranges scattered pieces of files on a hard disk for faster access
Copies important files and recovers them after loss
Prepares a disk and divides it into drives
Shows running programs and ends unresponsive ones
Controls network traffic in and out of the computer

blocks.html: Firmware is software permanently stored in a chip, such as the BIOS/UEFI that starts the computer (performs the POST and loads the OS), or the software inside a washing machine, router or TV remote.

rows: Whole high-level program → machine code at once; creates an executable file
High-level program line by line, running each line immediately

blocks.html: Two more system programs: the linker joins compiled program parts and libraries into one executable, and the loader places the executable into RAM to run it.

rows: MS Word, LibreOffice Writer, Google Docs
Playing or editing audio and video

blocks.html: Application software can also be grouped as:

items.html: General-purpose (packaged) — made for many users (Word, Excel).
Specific-purpose — for one kind of task (railway reservation, hospital management, payroll).
Customised (tailor-made / bespoke) — developed for one organisation's exact needs, such as a school's own fee and result software.

blocks.html: When you "buy" software, you usually buy a licence — permission to use it under certain rules. These rules are written in the End User Licence Agreement (EULA) that you accept during installation.

rows: MS Windows, MS Office, Adobe Photoshop
Many PDF readers and media players
Trial versions of utilities and games
Yes, and you may modify it

blocks.html: Free and Open-Source Software (FOSS) gives users four freedoms: to run the program for any purpose, to study how it works (source code), to change it, and to share copies, original or changed. Licences such as the GNU GPL protect these freedoms. Free here means freedom, not necessarily zero price.

Advantages of open source: no licence cost, can be customised, large community support, transparency and security through public review, no dependence on one company. Limitations: may need more technical skill, some professional features or support may be missing, compatibility issues with some file formats.

items.html: OEM (Original Equipment Manufacturer) licence — software pre-installed by the computer maker (e.g. Windows on a new laptop). It is tied to that machine and cannot be moved to another computer.
Retail licence — bought separately; can usually be moved to a new computer.
Volume licence — one licence for many computers in a school or company.
Subscription / SaaS (Software as a Service) — pay monthly or yearly and use software online or with automatic updates (e.g. online office suites).

blocks.html: Using or distributing software against its licence is software piracy, an offence under the Copyright Act and the IT Act.

items.html: Check system requirements — operating system version, processor, RAM, disk space, 32-bit or 64-bit.
Get it from a trusted source — the official website or app store (Microsoft Store, Google Play).
Run the installer (.exe or .msi on Windows), accept the EULA, choose the folder and options. Untick extra toolbars or unrelated programs.
Update regularly — updates and patches fix bugs and security holes; upgrades bring new versions.
Uninstall unused software from Settings → Apps → Installed apps (or Control Panel → Programs and Features). Do not just delete the folder.

blocks.html: Version numbers such as 3.2.1 usually mean major.minor.patch. An alpha version is an early internal test; a beta version is released to some users for testing before the final stable release.
Professional software is built through the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC):

items.html: Requirement analysis — understand what users need.
Design — plan the screens, data and program structure.
Coding — write the program in a language such as C++.
Testing — find and fix errors.
Deployment — install it for users.
Maintenance — fix problems and add features over time.

blocks.html: You will follow these same steps on a small scale in the project of Chapter 17.
Did you know? Android, the operating system on most smartphones in India, is built on the Linux kernel — so the student project Linus Torvalds began in 1991 now runs in almost every pocket.

lessons.title: Workshop 10: Explore the software on your computer

blocks.html: Aim: To identify, classify and manage software.

items.html: List installed software. Open Settings → Apps → Installed apps. Write 15 programs and classify each as system, application or programming software.
Find the OS details. Open Settings → System → About. Note the Windows edition, version and whether it is 32-bit or 64-bit.
Look at drivers. Open Device Manager (right-click Start). Expand Display adapters and Network adapters and note the driver names.
Run utilities. Run Disk Cleanup on drive C: and note how much space can be freed. Compress a folder into a ZIP file and compare sizes.
Licence hunt. For five programs, find out (from Help → About or the website) whether each is proprietary, freeware, shareware or open-source.
Install an open-source program (with your teacher's permission), such as LibreOffice or VLC, from its official website. Note the steps and the EULA.
Software is a set of programs, data and documentation; a program is a single set of instructions.
System software (OS, drivers, utilities, firmware, translators) runs the computer; application software does users' tasks; programming software helps build software.
Linux began in 1991 with Linus Torvalds, inspired by Tanenbaum's MINIX; it powers servers and Android.
Application software can be general-purpose, specific-purpose or customised.
Licences: proprietary, freeware, shareware, open-source, public domain, OEM, retail, volume and subscription; the EULA states the rules; piracy is illegal.
Software should be installed from trusted sources, kept updated and uninstalled properly.
The SDLC: requirement analysis, design, coding, testing, deployment and maintenance.
